long.title: A Year Without a Car
long.text:
When my old car finally broke down last January, the mechanic told me that repairing it would cost more than the car was worth. I was annoyed at first, because I had driven to work every day for ten years. But my sister suggested an experiment: why not try living without a car for a whole year? I laughed at the idea, but I agreed to try it for one month.
The first week was difficult. My office is eight kilometres from my flat, and I had to work out which buses to take. On the second day I got on the wrong one and arrived forty minutes late. My boss was not pleased. However, by the end of the week I had found a route that took only ten minutes longer than driving, and I could read on the bus instead of sitting in traffic.
After a month, I noticed some surprising changes. I was walking about six thousand more steps a day, and I slept better than I had for years. I was also saving money. Without paying for petrol, parking and insurance, I had almost two hundred dollars more each month. So I decided to continue the experiment.
Of course, there were problems. Shopping became more complicated, and I had to plan carefully before I went to the supermarket. Visiting my parents, who live in a village with only two buses a day, was the hardest part. A couple of times I had to borrow my sister's car, which she reminded me about often.
Now the year is over, and people keep asking me whether I will buy a new car. I'm still not sure. I miss the freedom of being able to go anywhere at any time, especially at weekends. But I don't miss the traffic or the cost. For now, I've bought a second-hand bicycle, and I've joined a car-sharing club for the occasional long journey. Perhaps that is the right balance for me.

qs.q: Why did the writer stop using the old car?
qs.a: It would cost too much to repair.
w: The writer's sister wanted to buy it.
The writer wanted to get more exercise.
qs.why: “repairing it would cost more than the car was worth.”

qs.q: What happened during the first week?
qs.a: The writer arrived late for work once.
w: The writer decided to stop the experiment.
The writer found a route faster than driving.
The writer's boss offered a lift to work.
qs.why: “On the second day I got on the wrong one and arrived forty minutes late.” Đường mới chậm hơn lái xe 10 phút, không nhanh hơn.
“I had almost two hundred dollars more each month.” Xe đạp mua cuối năm.

qs.q: What was the most difficult part of the year?
w: getting to the office on time
finding a bus to the supermarket
qs.why: “Visiting my parents, who live in a village… was the hardest part.”

qs.q: How does the writer feel at the end of the year?
qs.a: The writer has found a compromise that works for now.
w: The writer will definitely buy a new car soon.
The writer never wants to drive again.
The writer thinks everyone should give up their car.
qs.why: “For now, I've bought a second-hand bicycle… Perhaps that is the right balance for me.”

long.title: Learning on the Job
long.text:
Most cafés hire staff who already know how to make coffee and serve customers. The Green Door café in Hue does the opposite. Every one of its waiters, cooks and baristas is a young person who has never had a job before. The café is part of a training programme for teenagers who left school early, and after six months there, most of them go on to find work in hotels and restaurants.
The idea came from Minh Chau, a former hotel manager. 'When I was interviewing people for jobs, I met so many young people who were clever and hard-working but had no experience,' she explains. 'Nobody wanted to give them a chance, so they couldn't get experience. I wanted to break that circle.'
Trainees spend their mornings in a classroom above the café, where they study English, food safety and customer service. In the afternoons they work downstairs with real customers. Mistakes happen, of course. 'On my first day I dropped a whole tray of drinks,' laughs Nam, who is seventeen. 'I wanted to run away. But the customers were really kind, and my trainer showed me how to carry the tray properly.'
Customers seem happy to be part of the project. Many of them are tourists who have read about the café online, but there are also local office workers who come in every day. A small notice on each table explains the programme and asks customers to be patient. 'The coffee is excellent and the service is friendly,' says one regular customer. 'If it's a bit slow sometimes, I don't mind at all.'
The café does not make much profit, and it depends on donations to pay for the classes. Minh Chau admits that money is a constant worry. But she has no plans to give up. Last year, forty-two trainees finished the programme, and thirty-eight of them are now in full-time jobs. 'That number,' she says, 'is the only profit I really care about.'

qs.q: What is unusual about the Green Door café?
qs.a: None of its staff had worked before.
w: It only employs experienced hotel workers.
It is only open to tourists.
It trains people to open their own cafés.
qs.why: “a young person who has never had a job before.”

qs.q: Why did Minh Chau start the programme?
qs.a: She saw that young people could not get their first job.
w: She was unhappy working as a hotel manager.
She needed more staff for her hotel.
She wanted to teach English to tourists.
qs.why: “Nobody wanted to give them a chance, so they couldn't get experience.”

qs.a: Trainees get support when they make mistakes.
w: Trainees often leave after their first day.
The work is too difficult for most teenagers.
Trainees are not allowed to serve drinks.
qs.why: “the customers were really kind, and my trainer showed me how to carry the tray properly.”

qs.q: What do the customers think of the café?
qs.a: They accept that the service is sometimes slow.
w: They come mainly because the coffee is cheap.
They would prefer more experienced staff.
They find the notice on the tables annoying.
qs.why: “If it's a bit slow sometimes, I don't mind at all.”

qs.q: What is the writer's main purpose?
qs.a: to describe a project that helps young people find work
w: to advertise a new café to tourists
to explain how to become a hotel manager
to complain about the lack of jobs for teenagers
qs.why: Cả bài nói về chương trình giúp người trẻ có việc (38/42 người có việc).

long.title: Evening and weekend courses
long.text:
A  Riverside Cooking School
Learn to cook simple meals from around the world in our friendly kitchen. Classes are on Tuesday evenings and are suitable for complete beginners. You take home everything you make. The course lasts ten weeks and all ingredients are included in the price.
B  City Photography Club
Improve your photos with an experienced photographer. We meet every Saturday morning and visit a different part of the city each week. You need your own camera, but it doesn't have to be expensive; many members use their phones. Free for students.
C  Spanish for Travellers
A short, practical course for people who are going on holiday soon. In four evening lessons you'll learn how to order food, ask for directions and book a hotel room. Groups have no more than eight people, and online lessons are also available.
D  Hilltop Pottery Studio
Make your own cups, bowls and plates on our pottery wheels. We run weekend courses for adults with or without experience. We fire your work in our oven and you can collect it a week later. Please wear old clothes!
E  Get Fit Together
A course for people who want to get fit but hate gyms. We exercise outdoors in the park every Sunday morning, whatever the weather. Each session includes running, games and stretching. Bring a friend for free on your first visit.
F  First Steps in Coding
Build your own website in six weeks. You don't need any experience, but you must bring a laptop. Lessons are on Wednesday evenings at the public library, and our teachers are all professional software developers.
G  Creative Writing Workshop
Write stories and poems and share them with a small, friendly group. Each Thursday evening we read work by famous writers and then try their techniques ourselves. At the end of the course, the best stories are published in a small book.
H  Guitar for Beginners
Learn to play your favourite songs in just eight weeks. Lessons take place on Monday evenings, and guitars are provided, so you don't need to buy one. Classes are relaxed and fun, and there's no need to read music.

pm.q: Huy works long hours during the week and wants a creative hobby at the weekend. He would like to make things that he can use at home.
pm.why: D: weekend courses; make your own cups, bowls and plates.

pm.q: Clara is going to Madrid next month and wants to learn some useful phrases quickly. She would prefer to study at home.
pm.why: C: short course before a holiday; online lessons are available.

pm.q: Tom is a student with very little money. He enjoys being outside and wants to see parts of his city he doesn't know.
pm.why: B: free for students; visit a different part of the city each week.

pm.q: Lan wants to learn a musical instrument but doesn't own one. She is only free on Monday evenings.
pm.why: H: Monday evenings; guitars are provided.

pm.q: Peter wants to start a small online business and needs a website, but he has never done anything like this before.
pm.why: F: build your own website; no experience needed.

long.title: Places to stay
long.text:
A  Seaview Apartments
Modern apartments just two minutes' walk from the beach. Each one has a balcony with sea views and a small kitchen. There is a children's pool and a playground. In July and August, the minimum stay is one week.
B  The Old Mill
A quiet farmhouse in the countryside, ten kilometres from the nearest town. It is perfect for walkers, with paths starting at the front door. Dogs are welcome. You will need a car, as there are no buses.
C  City Central Hostel
Cheap rooms in the heart of the old town, close to museums, shops and the main station. Breakfast is included and there is a shared kitchen. Most rooms are shared, but there are a few private rooms.
D  Lakeside Cabins
Wooden cabins by a beautiful lake where you can swim, fish or hire a boat. The cabins are simple, with no TV or internet, so guests can really relax. Bicycles are available free of charge.
E  The Grand Hotel
A luxury hotel with a spa, two restaurants and a rooftop bar. All rooms have air conditioning. Business guests can use our meeting rooms, and there is fast internet throughout the building.
F  Mountain View Camping
A large campsite at the foot of the mountains. Bring your own tent or rent one of ours. There are hot showers, a small shop and walks with local guides every morning.
G  Riverside Bed and Breakfast
A family-run B&B in a small village by the river. Our home-cooked breakfasts are famous! There are only three bedrooms, so it is always peaceful. The village has a good bus service to the city.
H  Harbour Lofts
Stylish apartments above the fishing harbour, with views of the boats. Several excellent seafood restaurants are just outside the door. They are not suitable for young children because of the steep stairs.

pm.q: Mr and Mrs Lee want a peaceful holiday away from phones and computers. They love being on the water.
pm.why: D: no TV or internet; swim, fish or hire a boat.

pm.q: Ana is travelling alone with very little money and wants to visit as many museums as possible.
pm.why: C: cheap rooms close to museums.

pm.q: The Nguyen family have two young children who love swimming. They plan to stay for a week in the summer.
pm.why: A: children's pool; minimum stay one week in July and August.

pm.q: Jack wants to go walking with his dog every day. He has his own car.
pm.why: B: perfect for walkers; dogs are welcome; you will need a car.

pm.q: Sophie has to attend meetings during her trip and needs to send work emails every evening.
pm.why: E: meeting rooms and fast internet.

long.title: Books to read
long.text:
A  The Silent Forest
A thriller set in a dark Canadian forest, where a young detective searches for a missing scientist. The story moves fast and every chapter ends with a surprise. At over 500 pages, it is a long read, but most readers can't put it down.
B  Kitchen Stories
Part cookbook, part family history. The writer shares her grandmother's recipes from Vietnam together with stories about growing up in a busy restaurant. The recipes are simple and the photos are beautiful.
C  Running Further
An experienced athlete explains how anyone can train for their first marathon. Clear weekly plans, advice on food and sleep, and honest stories about the writer's own mistakes make this a practical guide.
D  Stars Above Us
A short, easy introduction to astronomy for teenagers. Colourful pictures and simple diagrams explain the planets, the stars and how telescopes work. Each chapter is only a few pages long.
E  The Last Summer
A gentle, funny novel about three old friends who spend one last summer together in a seaside town. Nothing very dramatic happens, but the characters are wonderful and the ending is moving.
F  Money Made Simple
A clear guide to managing your money, written for young people starting their first job. It explains saving, bank accounts and how to avoid debt without using complicated language.
G  Lost Cities
The true story of the archaeologists who discovered ancient cities in the jungle. Full of adventure and real photographs, it reads like a novel, but every word is true.
H  Laugh Out Loud
A collection of short, funny stories that you can read in five minutes each. It is perfect for reading on the bus or before bed, and a great present for anyone who needs cheering up.

pm.q: Minh enjoys exciting stories full of surprises, and he doesn't mind long books.
pm.why: A: every chapter ends with a surprise; over 500 pages.

pm.q: Rosa has just started her first job and wants to understand how to look after her money.
pm.why: F: for young people starting their first job.

pm.q: Ken loves history and real-life adventures, but he finds most history books boring.
pm.why: G: true story, full of adventure, reads like a novel.

pm.q: Lucy wants something she can read in short breaks on her way to work that will make her smile.
pm.why: H: short, funny stories; perfect for reading on the bus.

pm.q: David's son is thirteen and interested in space, but he doesn't like long books.
pm.why: D: astronomy for teenagers; each chapter is only a few pages long.

long.title: My Year as a Volunteer
long.text:
After I finished school, I didn't know what I wanted to study at university, so I decided to take a year off. My parents were worried that I would waste the time, but a friend of my mother's told me about a project that needed volunteers to help in a small library in the mountains in the north of the country. I had never lived away from home before, and I wasn't sure I would be any good at it, but I agreed to go for six months.

The first few weeks were difficult. The village was much colder than I had expected, and I had brought the wrong clothes. The library was just one room in the old school, and most of the books were in very bad condition. On my first day only two children came in, and they left after ten minutes because there was nothing they wanted to read.

I realised that I had to do more than sit behind a desk. I started a reading club on Saturday mornings and asked the children what they would like to read. Most of them wanted comics and books about animals, which the library didn't have. So I wrote to publishers and bookshops in the city, and to my surprise several of them sent boxes of books for free. Soon the room was full every weekend, and some parents began to come too.

In the end I stayed for a whole year instead of six months. When I left, the village organised a small party for me, and one of the girls from the reading club gave me a card that said she wanted to be a teacher. That was the moment I knew what I wanted to do with my own life. I'm now in my second year of a teaching degree, and I still visit the village every summer.

qs.q: Why did the writer decide to take a year off?
qs.a: She had not decided what to study.
w: Her parents wanted her to work.
She wanted to earn money for university.
A friend asked her to travel with him.
qs.why: I didn't know what I wanted to study at university.

qs.q: What problem did the writer have when she first arrived?
qs.a: She had not packed suitable clothing.
w: She could not find anywhere to live.
The library was closed for repairs.
The children did not speak her language.
qs.why: I had brought the wrong clothes.

qs.q: Why did the two children leave the library on her first day?
qs.a: The library had nothing that interested them.
w: They had to go back to school.
She asked them to be quiet.
qs.why: there was nothing they wanted to read.

qs.q: How did the writer get new books for the library?
qs.a: She asked companies to give them.
w: She bought them with her own money.
The parents brought them from home.
qs.why: I wrote to publishers and bookshops… several of them sent boxes of books for free.

qs.q: What helped the writer decide on her future career?
qs.a: a message from a child she had helped
w: a talk with the village teacher
a book she read in the library
qs.why: a girl… gave me a card that said she wanted to be a teacher. That was the moment I knew.

However, the other members {2} me feel welcome immediately. We meet twice a week and run together in the park. At first I couldn't run more than two kilometres without {3} a break, but the coach gave me a training plan and I soon {4} the difference. Last month I {5} part in my first ten-kilometre race. I didn't win, of course, but I finished in under an hour, which was my {6}. Now I can't imagine my week without running.

mc.text: Pho is now famous all over the world, but it has a fairly short {1}. Most historians {2} with the idea that it first appeared in northern Vietnam in the early twentieth century. At that time, it was sold by street sellers who {3} their kitchens on their shoulders. After 1954, many people moved south and {4} the dish with them. Cooks in the south added herbs and bean sprouts, and a new style was {5}. Today, people still argue about which version is better, but most agree on one thing: a good bowl of pho {6} on the quality of its broth.

open.title: My Favourite Place
open.text: There is a small lake {1} the edge of my town where I often go at weekends. It is not famous, and there {2} never many people there, which is why I love it. I usually take a book and sit under a tree for hours. Last summer I saw a family of ducks {3} the first time. I have been going there {4} I was a child, and it has hardly changed. I hope it stays {5} same for many years, because it is the place {6} I feel most relaxed.

gaps.why: on / at the edge of = ở rìa.
there are + số nhiều (many people).
for the first time = lần đầu.
since + mốc thời gian (I was a child).

open.title: An Email to a Friend
open.text: Hi Lan, thanks {1} your message. I'm sorry I didn't reply sooner, but I've been really busy {2} my exams. They finally finished yesterday, so now I can relax! Are you free {3} Saturday? There's a new film at the cinema that I'd love to see. If you don't like films, we {4} go to the beach instead. Let me know {5} you prefer. I'm really looking forward {6} seeing you. Love, Mai

gaps.why: thanks for = cảm ơn vì.

động từ khuyết thiếu để gợi ý: we could go.

open.title: Why We Yawn
open.text: Everyone yawns, but scientists still are not completely sure why we {1} it. One popular idea is that yawning helps to cool the brain. When our brains get too warm, we may yawn {2} order to take in cooler air. Another interesting fact is that yawning is 'catching'. If you see someone yawn, you are much more likely {3} yawn yourself. Some studies suggest that this happens more often between friends {4} between strangers. Even reading {5} yawning can make people yawn. Are you yawning now? If so, you are not the only {6}!

gaps.why: do it = làm việc đó (thay cho yawn).
in order to = để.
be likely to + V.
more often … than = thường hơn so với.

kwt.s1: I started learning English three years ago.

kwt.s1: Somebody stole my bike last night.
